title: Shadow Kernel Emulation Benchmark Protocol (SKEB) - 2026
author: Diego Rios
body:
Summary:
This document defines the Shadow Kernel Emulation & Benchmark Protocol (SKEB): a standardized lab procedure, metrics contract, and release-gate checklist for evaluating experimental GPU kernel behavior using an emulator/shadow runtime prior to any production rollout. SKEB reduces risk from kernel regressions that affect tail latency, KV-cache correctness, and scheduling fairness by validating kernels in a controlled shadow environment that mirrors production traffic shapes.

Goals and non-goals:
- Goals:
  - Provide a repeatable protocol to compare a candidate kernel against the incumbent across cost, latency tails, and failure modes.
  - Surface subtle interactions between scheduler admission signals, KV cache warmup patterns, and kernel memory fragmentation.
  - Produce a deterministic artifact (bench report) to inform release gating and rollback criteria.
- Non-goals:
  - This is not an exhaustive functional test suite for model correctness or model artifacts.
  - SKEB does not replace live canaries; it reduces the failure surface before canarying.

When to run SKEB:
1. New kernel rollout (any kernel that modifies memory allocation, batching, or attention implementation).
2. Scheduler policy changes that alter admission or preemption behavior.
3. Quantization/backing-store changes that affect execution pathing.

Overview of the protocol:
- Step 0: Define the experiment matrix (workloads, sequence length distributions, model variants, concurrency shapes).
- Step 1: Create a shadow-emulation environment that accepts production sampling traffic (mirrored or synthetic replay).
- Step 2: Run incumbent kernel baseline experiments (N runs), collect metrics and traces.
- Step 3: Run candidate kernel under identical load shapes (N runs).
- Step 4: Perform statistical comparison and regression detection using the metric contracts below.
- Step 5: Record artifacts and signoff results in the bench report.

Detailed procedure:
1) Experiment matrix (example):
   - Models: rwkv-14b-chi, gothic-7b, redwood-lite-3b (representative small/med/large).
   - Sequence length buckets: 32, 128, 512, 2048.
   - Concurrency shapes: steady (200 qps), bursty (spike to 2000 qps for 30s every 5m), idle-warmup (sustained 5 qps then jump to 250 qps).
   - KV-cache patterns: cold start, session-affinity warm, interleaved sessions.
   - Replication: 5 independent runs per cell with different random seeds for prompt corpus.

2) Environment setup:
   - Use the shadow-emulator image: registry.redwood.internal/runtime-shadow:2026-03.
   - Mirror production headers: add X-Shadow-Run: true.
   - Ensure identical HW topology emulation (same NUMA layout and GPU memory caps).
   - Disable external persistence writes; enable telemetry-forwarding to profiling cluster.

3) Data collection and required signals:
   - Latency percentiles: p50, p90, p95, p99, p99.9.
   - Kernel-level histograms: kernel-runtime-ms, kernel-queue-wait-ms, kernel-memory-fragmentation-ratio.
   - Scheduler signals: admission-wait-time-ms, preemption-count, priority-reassign-events.
   - KV cache metrics: kv-hit-rate, kv-warmup-time-ms, kv-eviction-rate.
   - Resource metrics: GPU SM utilization, GPU mem alloc/release-rate, host CPU sys/idle.
   - Error signals: soft-errors, OOM events, kernel-fallback-count.

4) CLI-run example:
   - Replayer command (synthetic):
     ./bench/replay --matrix=matrices/rec-14b.yaml --shadow-image=registry.redwood.internal/runtime-shadow:2026-03 --out=artifacts/run-20260301 --runs=5

5) YAML snippet (workload cell):
   - workload:
       model: rec-14b
       seq_lengths: [32,128,512,2048]
       qps_profile: bursty
       kv_pattern: interleaved

Artifact format (bench report):
- header: {kernel_candidate: <git_sha>, kernel_base: <git_sha>, hw_profile: <desc>, matrix_id: <id>}
- summary: short paragraph of primary regressions/improvements
- tables: per-model per-bucket metric deltas with CI
- traces: links to trace bundles and kernel flamegraphs
- verdict: pass | marginal | fail

Metric contracts and failure criteria (hard gates):
| Metric | Allowed delta | Gate type | Action if breached |
|---|---:|---|---|
| p99 latency | +10% absolute or +50ms | Hard | Block rollout; require triage run |
| p99.9 latency | +5% absolute or +100ms | Hard | Block rollout; create P0 investigation |
| kv-hit-rate | -2% absolute | Hard | Block rollout; verify cache correctness |
| OOMs per 10k requests | >0 | Hard | Block rollout; abort candidate |
| kernel-fallback-count | >1 per 1k requests | Hard | Block rollout; require deterministic repro |
| syst. GPU mem fragmentation ratio | +20% rel | Soft | Manual review; must justify with perf win elsewhere |

Statistical analysis guidance:
- Use bootstrap resampling (10k samples) for percentile confidence intervals.
- Require 95% CI non-overlap for claiming improvement. For regressions, any statistically significant worsening that also exceeds the metric contract must be treated as a hard failure.
- When results are marginal, run extended replay with production-mirror traffic for at least 6 hours.

Root-cause & triage playbook pointers:
1. If p99 regressions appear without kernel-fallbacks:
   - Inspect admission-wait-time and queue histograms.
   - Check for subtle changes in batch-slicing thresholds (compare kernel config headers).
2. If kv-hit-rate drops:
   - Replay with single-session traces to verify session-affinity bookkeeping.
   - Verify serialization of KV-touch operations in kernel path.
3. If memory fragmentation rises:
   - Record allocation/free size distribution and GC-like compaction triggers.
   - Test with synthetic constant-allocation microbench to isolate allocator behaviour.

Rollout gating and required signoff:
- Required signoffs: runtime-service-owner (engineering), profiling-lead, SRE oncall.
- Release gating matrix:
  1) Hard gates cleared -> candidate allowed to progress to limited canary (5% traffic).
  2) Canary must run for 24 hours with no hard-gate breaches and p99+ benchmarks within 3% of baseline.
  3) If canary passes, ramp per standard release plan.

Reporting and artifacts to attach to the release ticket:
- bench-report.json (machine readable summary),
- pprof flamegraphs for kernel hot paths,
- trace bundle links,
- raw telemetry shard keys and replay seed.

Safety notes and common pitfalls:
- Shadow runs do not perfectly reproduce hardware transient faults (thermal throttling, nvlink flakiness). Always run a short hardware health check on candidate nodes before canary.
- Avoid synthetic-only corpora: include at least one sampled production mirror segment for each critical workload.
- Watch for signal amplification: tiny preemption-count deltas can produce outsized tail effects under bursty traffic.

Maintenance and ownership:
- Owning team: eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling.
- SKEB stewardship: profiling-team (quarterly updates) and runtime release engineers (per-rollout updates).
- Add new workload matrices to matrices/ directory in bench repo with change MR and reviewer from owning team.

Appendix A: Quick checklist (pre-run)
1) Confirm matrix YAML exists and matches production model versions.
2) Ensure shadow-image tag matches candidate kernel git sha.
3) Allocate dedicated profiling cluster with 2x production memory headroom.
4) Verify telemetry pipeline is reachable (profiling ingestion health OK).

Appendix B: Example bench verdict summary (text):
- Candidate: kernel-shim@sha1abc
- Baseline: kernel-stable@sha0fff
- Result: marginal -> p99 +8% (45ms), p99.9 +160ms -> FAIL (blocked)
- Notes: increased preemption-count correlated with queue-wait spikes during bursty profile. Triage assigned to scheduler component.
